harriet-tubman.excerpt: In June 1863, Harriet Tubman guided three Union gunboats up a mined river. By morning, more than 700 people were free.
sections: Before the war

Harriet Tubman was born into slavery on Maryland's Eastern Shore around 1820. She escaped north in her late twenties, in 1849, and then went back, numerous times, to lead others out. Over about ten years on the Underground Railroad she guided roughly 70 people to freedom. In one night in 1863 she would help free ten times that number.
Nurse, scout, spy

By the start of 1863 Tubman was in South Carolina, sent at the request of the Governor of Massachusetts to Hilton Head, which the Union had captured early in the war. She worked first as a laundress and nurse, then was ordered to form a spy ring. She recruited scouts, eight of them according to History.com, who mapped the Combahee River country and carried word to the enslaved people on its plantations that freedom was coming. A freedom seeker named Francis Izzard, who reached Beaufort in May 1863, brought news of the Confederate mines, called torpedoes, planted in the river. Tubman could not read, so she memorised what the scouts reported.
The night of 1 June 1863

On the evening of 1 June 1863 three gunboats, the John Adams, the Harriet A. Weed and the Sentinel, left Beaufort for the Combahee. Tubman sailed on the John Adams with Colonel James Montgomery, commander of the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers, a Black regiment; about 300 soldiers took part, including some 50 men from a Rhode Island artillery unit. The Sentinel ran aground and its troops transferred to the other boats. Guided past the mines, the John Adams and the Harriet A. Weed reached the river's mouth at Fields Point early on 2 June, and the Confederate pickets fled.

As the boats came up the river, enslaved people ran from the fields towards them, carrying children and whatever they could. Soldiers in rowboats ferried them to the gunboats. Seven plantations were burned, with their rice mills, a cotton gin and a sawmill, and a pontoon bridge was shot to pieces. Tubman later described the scene herself; her own account, as retold by History.com, survives only in one source and is paraphrased here rather than quoted.
More than 700

By the morning of 2 June, more than 700 people were free. Sources give the count as 727, 750, 756 or 800; the National Park Service says more than 750. Many of the freed men enlisted: the Park Service says Tubman helped recruit more than 150 of them into the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers. A Boston newspaper, the Commonwealth, named Tubman as the raid's heroine in July 1863, and Harper's Weekly illustrated the escape that same month.

Tubman is often called the first woman in American history to lead a military raid. The US House of Representatives' history office puts it more carefully: she was the first African American woman to lead troops in a military operation, and she led the raid with Colonel Montgomery. That is the claim made here.
Two hundred dollars

For more than three years of service Tubman was paid about 200 dollars. In 1865 she asked her Auburn neighbour, Secretary of State William Seward, for help; nothing came of it. In 1874 a bill for 5,000 dollars was introduced in Congress; a committee cut it to 1,600, and neither version reached a vote. She received a pension only as the widow of Nelson Davis, a Black Union veteran she married after the war: eight dollars a month from 1892. In 1899, after a House committee called hers "a very deserving case", President McKinley signed a bill raising it to twenty dollars; the Senate had refused the twenty-five the House proposed. Historian Kate Clifford Larson says she was denied a soldier's pension because she was a woman.

Tubman spent her last years in Auburn, New York, where she opened a home for elderly Black people and campaigned for women's votes. She died in 1913 and was buried with military honours in Fort Hill Cemetery.

henry-box-brown.excerpt: He had himself nailed into a crate and shipped to freedom: 26 hours in the dark, part of it upside down.
sections: Richmond

Henry Brown was born into slavery in Louisa County, Virginia, in 1815 or 1816, one of eight children enslaved by John Barret, a former mayor of Richmond. When Barret died in 1830, Henry was sent to Richmond to work in the tobacco factory of Barret's son. He became a skilled tobacco worker, and by working extra hours earned enough to rent a house. Around 1836 he married Nancy, who was enslaved by another man, and they had three children; the family sang in the choir of the First African Baptist Church.
In August 1848 Nancy's enslaver sold her and the three children to a man in North Carolina. She was pregnant with a fourth. Brown resolved to leave Virginia in a way no one would expect.
This side up with care

A fellow choir member, James Caesar Anthony Smith, a free Black man, introduced Brown to Samuel Alexander Smith, a white shoemaker who agreed to help for a fee. Samuel Smith wrote ahead to James Miller McKim of the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society in Philadelphia. On 23 March 1849 the two Smiths sealed Brown into a wooden box about three feet long, two feet wide and two and a half feet deep, labelled dry goods and marked "This side up with care". The drawing in Brown's own 1849 narrative reads "Right side up with care"; William Still's 1872 account gives the first wording.

The box went to Adams Express, a private shipping company, and travelled by rail to Aquia Creek, by steamboat up the Potomac to Washington, and on to Philadelphia. The label did not help much: at the transfers the box was handled roughly, and for several hours it sat upside down, Brown on his head. He stayed silent. The journey took about 26 hours; Britannica says 27.
Philadelphia, 24 March 1849

Early on 24 March the box reached the Anti-Slavery Society office, where McKim and others opened it. Brown climbed out alive and sang a hymn based on Psalm 40. He later wrote that he had risen, as it were, from the dead. A greeting he is said to have offered on climbing out appears only in Still's account and is not quoted here; a distance of 350 miles given on popular sites is not in our sources.

In May 1849 he spoke at the New England Anti-Slavery Convention in Boston, where he was renamed Henry Box Brown, and in September his Narrative, written with Charles Stearns, was published. Samuel Smith tried to ship two more men north that May, was caught, and was sentenced to six and a half years in the Virginia penitentiary.
The Mirror of Slavery

Brown commissioned a moving panorama, a long painted canvas unrolled before an audience, called Henry Box Brown's Mirror of Slavery, which opened in Boston in April 1850. In August 1850, as the Fugitive Slave Bill neared passage, he was attacked in the street in Providence, Rhode Island. In October he and James Smith sailed for England, exhibiting the panorama in Liverpool and Manchester that winter. In 1851 the partnership ended in a dispute over money; Smith complained that Brown had made no effort to buy his family's freedom.
Showman

Brown stayed in Britain for 25 years and became a showman. He toured the panorama through the 1850s, performed as an "African Prince" in fine clothes, won a libel case in 1852 against a newspaper that had printed racial slurs about his shows, and from about 1859 performed as a mesmerist, billing himself in Wales as "King of all the Mesmerisers". He remarried; his wife's name is not recorded. In 1875 he returned to the United States with her and their daughter Annie as "Prof. H. Box Brown", a magician whose act still ended with him climbing into his original box.
Henry Box Brown died in Toronto on 15 June 1897. Whether he ever saw Nancy and the children again is often stated with certainty; our sources do not settle it, so no claim is made here.
